html:
Würzburg. The last time I was here was at the end of March 2014, to celebrate our fourth anniversary as a couple. I posted about it on WeChat Moments and managed to write “sex on the beach” (the cocktail) as “sex on the bitch.” In the blink of an eye, next March will be our tenth anniversary.

The thing about European cities is that they barely change in decades, even centuries. Except, of course, cities like Rotterdam that tore it all up and started over.


My two visits to Würzburg had completely different purposes, and my life has changed a lot in between.
Last time it was an anniversary vacation. I had been abroad, and in my PhD, for barely six months. I was still stumbling through German, taking courses to fill the gaps in my knowledge, and trying with all my might to fit in with the Germans. Back then my goal was to defend my thesis in German.
This time it’s a business trip, a five-hour drive from the Netherlands. I finished my PhD more than a year ago. Obviously I didn’t defend in German, and I never quite fit in with the Germans either. I’ve been working for almost a year, I’m in Germany all the time, and I’ll be back again the week after next.

Downtown Würzburg


Life is funny like that. I remember that after my first visit to my current company three years ago, I said I’d definitely never end up there. Famous last words. A few days ago my boss gave me a permanent contract, and when I got it I didn’t feel much of anything. I had been just a tiny bit worried beforehand. I knew it would be fine, but my boss is autocratic and moody, so nothing he did would have surprised me. He does think highly of me, though, and we spent ages talking about the Chinese market.

Only once things are settled do you have the drive to do your work properly. Today’s customer visit went smoothly and was cordial from start to finish. There’s a Chinese guy at the company, and when we got to talking about Zhihu, China’s answer to Quora, and went to follow each other, it turned out he already followed me. We were both surprised: he felt he was meeting an “internet celebrity,” and I was meeting, for the first time, a fellow acoustician who follows me on Zhihu. My first time as an “internet celebrity.” I was touched and happy. It means all that typing wasn’t for nothing: somebody really does read it.

After the visit, a German colleague of theirs saw me out, and we talked about our previous jobs. He spent six years in academia and moved here just over six months ago. Family was one reason, but more importantly, in academia work and life were impossible to separate; now, the moment five o’clock comes, he switches straight into off-duty mode. If he hadn’t been a customer, I’d have given him a high five. I couldn’t agree more! Writing articles on Zhihu, running the WeChat account, reading up on economics and so on: I started all of it after I began working. In academia, everything except papers felt like idle reading, and reading it made me feel guilty. Since I started working, I meet different customers and see different needs, and I’ve come to understand acoustics in far more practical terms. That more realistic understanding gives what I learn more direction and more drive. Back at the university I wasn’t really sure what acoustics was actually for, and I felt lost about the future. Since I started working, I see the industry more and more clearly, and many things I never thought about, or never dared to think about, no longer seem so far out of reach.

As the head of the customer’s acoustics group said today: the moment you try to cut costs, noise problems appear, so acoustic engineers will never be out of a job. The company has more than two thousand employees worldwide, and over a hundred of them work in acoustics. That number is astonishing; acoustics really is getting more and more attention. The customer supplies the car manufacturers. With electric vehicles all the rage, the annoying engine noise is gone, but high-frequency problems that it used to mask now stand out. So the OEMs have set suppliers at every tier scrambling to solve them. A while ago I talked with a supplier in China that is building an acoustics lab and buying equipment on a large scale. So it seems that, just as he said, acoustic engineers won’t be out of work any time soon.

The Main river. Tomorrow’s customer is just nearby.

All the driving plus the customer visit has worn me out a bit, and somehow this turned into an essay. I rather like it. Between serious popular-science pieces (sometimes not so serious), writing something informal is quite relaxing.

Tomorrow I visit another customer. The week after next I’ll be at the International Congress on Acoustics (ICA) in Aachen, and after that I’m heading back to China for the national acoustics conference in Shenzhen and the automotive testing expo in Shanghai. If you’re going too, give me a shout. I’m looking forward to meeting more of you!
